query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Partial-annealing treatments that increase local atomic ordering in as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys will broaden the first-order magnetostructural transition and reduce hysteresis, dominating magnetocaloric performance more strongly than composition changes alone.
generation.material_initial_state: Thin-film or foil-like as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys for magnetic refrigeration (without rare-earth elements).
generation.intervention: Perform systematic post-deposition annealing at controlled temperatures (300–600 °C) and durations (e.g., 15–60 min) to tune local ordering.
generation.conditions: Samples are initially sputter-deposited onto suitable substrates; a range of partial-annealing conditions is applied. Magnetocaloric measurements are conducted under low applied fields (~0.5–2 T).
generation.structural_mediator: Increased atomic ordering in the as-deposited grains and reduced structural/chemical inhomogeneities, as induced by thermal treatment.
generation.mechanism: Thermally induced ordering and reduced defect density shift and broaden the magnetostructural transition, decreasing intrinsic hysteresis by improving magnetic homogeneity and stabilizing the intermediate transformation state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, partially annealed samples will exhibit a broader magnetotransformation interval, reduced hysteresis losses, and a comparable or slightly lower peak entropy-change value under low magnetic fields, consistent with improved local ordering.
generation.baseline: As-deposited samples that exhibit a sharper transition with larger hysteresis and slightly higher peak magnetocaloric entropy change under low-field cycling.
generation.boundary: These effects should be most pronounced for annealing treatments between 300–600 °C and for moderate field strengths up to ~2 T; excessively high temperatures or prolonged annealing times may induce secondary phases or coarsening that alters the response in other ways.
generation.uncertainty: We cannot quantify the exact magnitude of hysteresis reduction or peak-broadening without further experimental data, and composition variations or processing differences may also influence outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate and divide a single batch of as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films into multiple groups, each subjected to distinct partial-annealing conditions (different temperatures/durations). Measure magnetocaloric characteristics (isothermal magnetization, entropy change, hysteresis) and microstructural ordering (e.g., XRD peak widths) across the samples.
measurements: X-ray diffraction peak profiles to assess changes in structural disorder
Calorimetric measurements to quantify entropy change
Low-field magnetization loops to measure magnetic hysteresis
Characterization of transformation temperature range and sharpness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the as-deposited and partially annealed samples show no consistent broadening of the magnetostructural transition or change in hysteresis, then the hypothesis that local ordering (via controlled annealing) dominates these properties would be falsified.

As shown below, this corresponds to an increase in the magnetic homogeneity of the samples. A large FWHM may indicate strain and/or chemical inhomogeneities induced by the arc-melting and cold rolling process. The large FWHM could also indicate very small grains as one might see in a ball milling process. Our samples have been brutalized, a testament to their ductility and production worthiness, and as such there should be effects of strain, defects (both vacancies and stacking faults), and grain size reduction. All three of these effects would decrease with annealing leading to a sharpened diffraction peak. The addition of Pd has similar effects on the magnetic homogeneity as annealing. However, the broadening of the XRD peaks with Pd content does not appear consistent with this trend. It is possible that the damage done to the surface of the sample during cold-rolling is not indicative of the bulk and that Pd aids in reducing defects. The behavior of the entropy change peak and refrigerant capacity with applied field were fit to power functions (Fig. 5), namely −ΔSmax ∝ Hn and RC ∝ Hm; mean field theory predicts n = 2/3 and m = 4/3. We annotate these exponents with subscripts that describe the heat treatment (annealed or unannealed) and Pd content. Figure 6 shows resulting values of n and m for all samples as a function of Pd atomic percent. For the entropy change, n is always sublinear, and decreases with both Pd and annealing: nu,0% = 0.86 falls to nu,5.88% = 0.81 with Pd added, while annealing reduces the exponent: na,0% = 0.84. The behavior of RC is nearly linear with field for the unannealed, x = 0 sample (mu,0% = 0.99), but becomes superlinear with 6% Pd added (mu,5.88% = 1.10). Annealing further increases m, with ma,0% = 1.05 and ma,5.88% = 1.13. These results imply that the improvement of the refrigerant capacity with Pd has less to do with overall magnitude of the entropy change and more with the increased susceptibility of the material near the phase transition. cited_evidence.text: where Tpeak is the temperature at ΔSmax for each field, and TR is the temperature at 75% of ΔSmax above Tpeak. As shown in Fig. 7 for x = 0.12% and x = 2.91%, the curves do not collapse onto a single curve. It is apparent by visual inspection, though, that the degree of collapse increases when Pd is added. We can quantify the degree of collapse using statistical methods, namely the Brown-Forsythe analysis of variance (BF method). The BF method gives a single statistic, F, which directly measures the homogeneity of variance between a group of peaked curves. F is zero when a group of curves is identical, and increases from there as the set of curves becomes more inhomogeneous. This therefore gives us direct evidence that distributions of exchange interactions exist in the material: a small distribution will be essentially a perfect homogeneous material, and will have F approaching zero; a broad distribution will lead to increased F. We observe a decrease in F of at least 50% with annealing or Pd incorporation, and an additional 50% decrease with both annealing and adding Pd content. chosen.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that the degree of local ordering, tunable via partial annealing, governs both the breadth of the magnetostructural transition and the magnitude/hysteresis of the magnetocaloric response—more so than simple bulk composition changes alone. A distinct shift or broadening of the first-order transition under these controlled thermal treatments, especially with reduced hysteresis, would corroborate the proposed mechanism; unchanged hysteresis despite modified ordering, however, would refute it.
